column1: # Containers as DATA: what the step loop evaluates, and what it leaves
# alone. The bracket forms are documented in core/spec/README.md — `[ … ]`
# and `{ … }` are the PARSER's containers (Eval set), `[q … ]` and
# `{q … }` the runtime's, and `p( … )` is a paren-EXPRESSION value rather
# The eval/no-eval split is the whole subject, and writing these rows found
# two defects in core/ts. It descended into a map REGARDLESS of the Eval
# flag, so a map a word handler returned had its values evaluated on one
# side and not the other — `{q a: [ boomq 1 ] }` RAISED in TS where Go
# returned the map untouched. And a map value that evaluated to NOTHING
# kept its key as an empty list where Go drops the key entirely.
# --- the Eval flag decides, for lists and maps alike -----------------------
# A container the PARSER built evaluates its contents once, at the end of
# the run; one a word handler returned is data and stays verbatim. Quoting
# the OUTER container stops the descent — the inner one is not reached, so
# its own flag never gets a say.
# --- an error inside a container propagates — but only if reached ----------
# The same program under the two flags: evaluated, the handler's code
# reaches the caller; unevaluated, the words are inert data. This pair is
# --- what a map VALUE may be, and how many residuals it leaves -------------
# A list value stays a LIST of its residuals; a paren-expr or a bare word
# COLLAPSES to a single residual, or to a list when it leaves several. Zero
# residuals DROPS the key — `{a: ()}` is `{}`, not `{a:[]}`, which is the
# --- nesting, and the residual layout around a container -------------------
# A container is one value on the stack however deep it goes, and a
# multi-return word inside one lays every result into the enclosing list.
# Nothing to evaluate is not an error, and a scalar element passes through
# --- the `list` kind carries the same structure notation -------------------
# So a row can pin a nested value's RENDER without running it.
# --- a RUNTIME map handed to a word is data, at consumption too ----------
# The Eval gate applies where a map is CONSUMED as an argument, not only at
# the end-of-run residual sweep. core/ts gated the residual path and not the
# consumption path, so a `{q …}` map passed to a word had its values
# evaluated anyway — `boomq {q a: p( nosuchword ) }` raised undefined_word
# from inside the map where Go hands the handler the map as given and lets
run boomq {q a: { b: p( nosuchword ) } }
run boomq {q a: {q b: p( nosuchword ) } }
# An END or paren marker written where a map value goes is a PROGRAM, not
# data: running it is what drops the key, because an End alone leaves no
# residual. core/ts enumerated only paren-exprs and words as programs, so
# the marker fell through and was stored — `{ a: ; }` rendered `{a:end}`
# against Go's `{}`, and a stray `)` became map data instead of the syntax
# --- a map ARGUMENT is evaluated before the handler runs ----------------
# So a failure inside the map is reported instead of the handler's own
# error masking it. Two defects made core/ts fire first: a bare WORD map
# value went through resolveWordsDeep, which leaves an unresolvable name
# ALONE, where Go runs it in a sub-engine (a def resolves, an unbound name
# raises); and the NESTED-map arm carried no Eval gate, so a runtime map
# inside an eval one was evaluated anyway.
# The pairs below are the point: which error surfaces says which side ran
# first, and the {q …} rows say the gate is respected all the way down.
run boomq { a: addq b: p( nosuchword ) }
run boomq { a: nosuchword b: p( addq 1 ) }
run boomq { a: p( ) b: nosuchword }
run boomq { a: {q b: p( nosuchword ) } }
